en: The *Vinaya-śīla-mūla-ṭīkā* (Commentary on the Root Verses of the Vinaya Precepts) uses the term "precepts" (*śīla*) as its title. Regarding the practice of begging for and wearing cut-and-sewn robes (*khaṇḍa-cīvara*),
it is named according to this single principle [of the precepts], and thus the names are identical.
Because of this honorable title, they are called *bhikṣus*.
[Omitted text] Because they have attained only a small measure of realization, they are termed "semblances."

The statement that "in the causal stage, one must already possess the distant, conditioned, and untainted [dharmas]" clarifies that the one who has severed the fetters is fully endowed with unconditioned merit.

The remaining four [karmas] may be understood accordingly. Regarding the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations), the mental formulation is as follows:
[The text here indicates that] when the four conditions are complete, it constitutes the ritual for conferring the status of a renunciant (*pravrajyā*).

Therefore it is said: [As for] within the boundary, not forming a separate assembly... four persons receiving the precepts whose years are full... what is accomplished? Regarding the "sufficient text" and the "sufficient middle," the bhikṣu therein... accomplishes the attainment of the place.

This text refers to that which is within the boundary (*sīmā*). [The characters are obscured: ... by means of negation one reveals the correct; because there is no [affirmative] revelation, one attains the precept. This is the meaning of the precept.
The "one precept" refers to non-action (*avijñapti*) and the cessation of evil.

Although [the text] is fragmentary, it is said that the precepts are "equal" because the preceding phrase prohibits the seven [paths of action] of body and speech, while the subsequent three phrases clarify the prevention of the three poisons.
What is meant by "not abandoning"?

From the beginning up until "not the seed of nakedness," it clarifies that [the two] mutually abandon one another.
The third section, from "If one further speaks other words" (*yadi punar anyathā-vādaṃ kuryāt*) down to "this is called" (*ity ucyate*),
clarifies the disparagement of the Triple Gem, the abandonment [of the path], and the pursuit of what is direct, [as well as] the weariness with the path.

First, regarding the joy of remaining at home despite poverty... [omitted] ...as stated below, this does not yet explicitly clarify the relinquishment of the precepts... [omitted] ...the two abodes within the realm of animals are likewise...
[omitted] ...explained in detail, up to and including the case of men, which is also thus.
Whether there is an obstruction or no obstruction is likewise as previously stated. Thus far, although the gravity of the offense has not yet been clarified, it follows accordingly.
Within the sphere [of the offense], there are four permutations.
The first part clearly sets forth the three realms as the objects [of the offense].
The second part, from "Furthermore, there are five kinds" onwards,
concludes with the statement that committing unchaste acts in these five locations constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding the five types within the single destination (*ekāyana*):
the third begins from "furthermore, there are five kinds" below,
and concludes with the section on the three types of women and the three types of men.
The case of committing an act of impurity within this [context] constitutes a *pārājika* offense;
this has already been explained above, clarifying its application and enumeration.
Fourth, from the section concerning the three locations of a person's wife downward.
The two cases for male animals are likewise concluded. Thus far,
regarding the non-appropriate objects of action,
there are six hundred and twenty-four permutations concerning the non-appropriate spheres of activity.
A human woman, a non-human woman, and an animal woman;
a human female, a non-human female, and an animal female;
a human hermaphrodite, a non-human hermaphrodite, and an animal hermaphrodite.
There is one set of three "three-pronged gates" (*sang-ch'ang men*).
Within each three-pronged gate, there are four internal divisions of four phrases;
thus, across the three three-pronged gates, there are twelve [divisions].
Nine times nine makes twelve phrases;
in total, there are one hundred and eight phrases.
These concern human hermaphrodites, non-human hermaphrodites, and animal hermaphrodites.
There is a human male and a non-human male.
Regarding the human eunuch, there are two apertures above;
within one of these apertures, there is an internal partition consisting of four phrases.
In the second section on the creation of the gates,
there are eight phrases; thus, there are six sets of eight phrases,
totaling forty-eight phrases.
Calculating the previous one hundred and eight phrases,
there are altogether one hundred and fifty-six phrases;
within awakening, there are one hundred and fifty-six.
In the state of sleep there are one hundred and fifty-six;
at the moment of initial death there are one hundred and fifty-six,
for the most part not yet disintegrated.
There are one hundred and fifty-six [cases] in the first category;
in total, there are six hundred and twenty-four phrases.
Within the section on the coercion by enemies, from the wives of men down to animals and those with both sexual organs, there is one [category].
The first [section] has nine [parts].
The first [part] contains three gates of higher [attainment].
Within each gate of higher attainment, there are seven phrases concerning the experience of pleasure during the three periods of time.
The three gates of creation comprise twenty-one phrases;
each phrase contains four internal sub-phrases,
totaling eighty-four phrases.
First, there are eighty-four phrases; ninth, there are nine sets of eighty-four phrases.
Nine times eight is seventy-two, which constitutes seven hundred and twenty phrases.
The four times nine makes thirty-six phrases;
in total, there are seven hundred and fifty-six phrases.
From humans and eunuchs up to animals and eunuchs, there are six categories combined.
First, there are two "wound-gates" above.
Within one wound, there are seven phrases concerning experiencing pleasure or non-pleasure during three periods.
Within the second wound-gate, there are two sets of seven, totaling fourteen phrases.
Within each phrase there are four internal divisions,
making sixteen phrases in total.
When these six aspects are combined, there are fifty-six phrases.
Five times six is thirty-six;
thus, there are three hundred and thirty-six phrases in total.
When the three faculties and two faculties are combined, there are one thousand nine hundred and twenty phrases.
There are one thousand nine hundred and twenty [breaths] during the waking state,
and one thousand nine hundred and twenty during sleep;
at the onset of death, for the most part, they have not yet ceased.
Each contains one thousand nine hundred and two phrases,
totaling four thousand three hundred and sixty-eight phrases. In these cases,
the enemy takes the bhikṣu himself as the object.
The bhikṣu has two gateways of wounds.
In the first gateway of wounds, there are seven phrases concerning pleasure and non-pleasure during the three periods;
in the second, there are fourteen phrases.
Each line contains four internal divisions,
totaling fifty-six lines.
When multiplied by the four thousand four hundred twenty-four ways in which an enemy might forcibly constrain one, there are a total of forty-four thousand two hundred twenty-four lines.
Regarding the determination of offenses,
there are cases where the offense is consummated through the preliminary effort,
and there are cases where the gravity of the offense varies.
It is like a person who has internal lustful thoughts; though their mind,
governed by untrained wisdom, desires to violate a beautiful woman and moves their physical demeanor,
they have not yet left their original place.
If the mind ceases because the conditions have changed,
then by this very thought one incurs the *duṣkṛta* offense of a preparatory act;
one must perform the threefold confession before another person.
If the mind does not cease and one leaves the original place until the hands and bodies of both parties have grasped each other;
or if the conditions for the offense change and the mind wavers, it is a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) for the preceding act of seizing.
If one has completed the preparatory act, it is a light *sthūlātyaya*;
one should repent before a small group.
If the mind has not yet ceased [from the intention], [the offense remains as described].
If the male and female sexual organs touch one another but have not yet entered the body,
and one subsequently ceases the mind [of desire], one commits a heavy *sthūlātyaya* of preliminary effort (*prayoga*).
One must repent before the great assembly within the boundary (*sīmā*).
If, moreover, the mind does not cease,
and the two forms are both grasped, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense based on the preceding lightness or heaviness;
once the volitional thought (*cetanā*) is completed, it becomes a grave offense of ultimate fruition (*niṣṭhā-guru-pāpa*).
Having no further destination,
it is called ultimate;
it acts as a cause for others.
This is called skillful means (upāya).
If one perceives what is not the Path as the Path, or if one has doubt [regarding it], [it is not skillful means].
In these two cases, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*).
One should repent before a small group [of monks].
This applies from when a corpse is half-decomposed or worse, down to the stage where only bones remain.
If one falsely forms the perception of a path regarding the ears, nose, or even within a *kuṇḍikā* (water flask),
one commits a light *sthūlātyaya* offense of ultimate completion.
If one thinks that the object is real,
or if one doubts whether the object is real,
one commits a light *sthūlātyaya* offense of preliminary preparation (*prayoga*).
Within the seven categories [of offenses], there are *sthūlātyaya* and *duṣkṛta*.
These two names apply generally to both the culmination and the preliminary stages;

however, in the case of mere *duṣkṛta*, although it is a preliminary stage, it does not serve as the cause for the first two [categories] or for the *parivāsa* (probation) or *mānāpya* (rehabilitation).
It serves as the cause for the ultimate *sthūlātyaya*;
this is merely because the names of the cause and the effect are identical.
All causes of a *sthūlātyaya* are, in fact, *duṣkṛta*.
How is this known?
Because a *sthūlātyaya* offense is not established;
for the second time, four admonitions are prescribed for a single precept.
If one abandons [the offense] after the first announcement and the second *karmavācanā* have been completed,
one must confess three *sthūlātyaya* offenses;
furthermore, it is not stated that there is a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
If one abandons [the undertaking] before the formal announcement (jñapti) is completed,
it is said that there is a duṣkṛta offense which must be confessed;
by this, it is verified and known.
When a *sthūlātyaya* is completed, there is no *dukkaṭa* to be confessed;
therefore, it is known that if one confesses after the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the second *karmavācana* have been concluded,
one must confess three *sthūlātyayas*.
Thus, we know that the *sthūlātyaya* does not constitute [the full offense].
The single term *duṣkṛta* also applies to both cause and effect.
Why, then, is it said that by taking the cause as the result, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*?
This is the most minor offense;
there is no other name for an offense more minor than this.
Therefore, one may take up the fruit based on the cause without committing an offense.
Below is the fifth section on "Opening [the Path] Without Offense.
This precept against sexual misconduct consists of these five sections;
all other subsequent precepts likewise consist of these five sections.
The Second Precept on Stealing. In the Vinaya, there are two [categories]:
robbery and theft, which is taking what is not given.
Of these three names, "robbery" (kai) is defined by the act of seizing through force.
"Stealing" refers to the fear of being discovered.
"Taking what is not given" means that the proponent of the doctrine does not relinquish it, thereby constituting a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
To destroy another's property with a mind of anger constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is intended to clarify that according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, one incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*),
whereas the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* treats it as a light offense because it discusses only the initial intention.
Because this Vinaya treatise concludes at this point, one incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).
These cases all differ in how they are explained by the two schools (*nikāya*);
if explained in full detail, both schools would incur two offenses.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"Stealing property belonging to the Three Jewels all constitutes a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*);
according to other vinayas, such violations constitute a *sthalanta*."
Regarding the violation of the precepts through committing grave offenses,
the reason they are not the same is,
in my view, as follows:
Regarding those who commit a grave offense according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:
when stealing property belonging to the Buddha or the Dharma from its guardians, one incurs a grave offense (*pārājika*) in all cases.
In other Vinayas, stealing property belonging to the Buddha or the Dharma constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
To speak directly regarding the Dharma: if one steals from an object that is not subject to the precepts, one incurs only a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
it does not matter whether one has stolen from the side of a person who guards it.
If one wishes for a broad explanation of these two categories, [it is as follows].
In all cases, there should be two offenses.
There are two types of grave offenses for stealing property belonging to the Sangha:

first, property belonging to the Sangha of the four directions; [second, property belonging to a specific monastery]. If one steals [the former] to the extent that it reaches five coins, it constitutes a grave offense.
According to all the Vinayas, one should incur two grave offenses in every case:
one grave offense against the *prajñapti-saṃgha* (the nominal Saṃgha),
and another grave offense against the guardian of the monastery.
If one steals property belonging to the *saṃgha* currently present, one also commits two offenses.
However, regarding the person guarding it, if the value reaches five *māṣaka*, one incurs one grave offense.
Since it is said to be "property currently being distributed," [the distinction applies].
Calculatedly stealing one person’s property constitutes another *sthūlātyaya* offense.
The precept against stealing also consists of five sections of text.
The first begins from the outset and concludes with the passage "until the True Dharma remains for a long time."
The section from "Explaining the causes and conditions for the arising [of offenses]" down to "not living together" explains the actual formulation of the precepts (*śikṣāpada*).
The third [section], from "from the meaning of a bhikṣu as above" down to "regarding ownerless objects worth less than five māsakas," provides a detailed explanation.
The fourth [section], from "a bhikṣuṇī" down to "it is deemed a transgression," completes the discussion.
This clearly explains the general conclusion regarding the five groups [of offenses].
The fifth section, from "one who does not commit an offense" onwards until the point where it is not yet explained,
clarifies the exemptions for non-offenses.
Within the section on causes and conditions, there are three parts.
The first, from the beginning up until the point where he builds a grass hut and returns with it,
clarifies the causal circumstances for constructing the grass hut.
The second section, from "Now I myself possess the craft and tools" below, until "this is precisely what is appropriate," clarifies the circumstances of constructing a tiled house.
The third section, from "At that time, in the kingdom of Magadha" below, until "the True Dharma shall abide for a long time," [clarifies the establishment of the monastery].
This explains the causes and conditions for stealing the property of a king.
Within the third section, the detailed exposition, there are two parts.
The first part, from the beginning up to "not living together," has already been explained as above.
This is a brief explanation of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.

Second, from the passage beginning with "There are three kinds of taking what is not given" down to "taking ownerless objects worth less than five coins," the act of taking what is not given is explained in detail.
Regarding the second section, which extensively explains *adattādāna* (taking what is not given), there are three sub-sections.
The first begins from the start and concludes with the statement, "This constitutes the six ways of acquiring [stolen property] that result in a *pārājika* offense."
This briefly clarifies taking what is not given.
From the second section, "Regarding the place," down to "I shall look after the path," it extensively explains taking what is not given by following the specific circumstances.
Third, from "seeking through skillful means" down to "less than five coins," the end of the passage clarifies the mental resolve regarding taking what is not given.
Within this concise explanation of taking what is not given, there are three subordinate points.
The first three phrases clarify the karmic act of stealing;
the second three phrases, "the perception that the object is not one's own," clarify the intention to steal;
and the third consists of three types of appropriation.
From "another's property" through "the perception of it as another's property," the end;
this clarifies the object stolen.
Regarding "another's property" and "the perception of it as another's property":
One who holds a person's entrusted property and then steals it for themselves,
such that the object belongs to the person to whom it was entrusted,
is therefore said to be "another's property."
One does not yet perceive it as another's possession.
Regarding the perception of another's possession:
suppose a thief has plundered another's goods and is crossing a guarded pass; when pursued by guards, the thief immediately abandons them with a mind of renunciation.
The original owner has again lost his mind;
since the officials do not regard this object as their own property,
it is therefore called "belonging to another."
Because one guards this object for the sake of its reward, it is called "protected by another.
If a bhikṣu steals this object,
he incurs an offense only against the person who guards it.
Because both the original owner and the thief have both developed a mind of relinquishment,
the phrase "one who has an owner and the perception that there is an owner" refers generally to all owners of property.
This is because both the object and [the intention] are present before one.
Even if the object were not present before one,
it is still termed "present" provided the owner lacks the intention to relinquish it.
If one steals these objects, one incurs guilt toward their owner.
As for the property of the Triple Gem, the Triple Gem itself is the owner;
therefore, it may all be considered as having an owner.
The items taken up above have not yet constituted the offense of theft; rather,
the result has been described in terms of its cause.
From the third fivefold set onwards,
the text correctly explains the accomplishment of theft;
within the "increase of six," it merely cites again the first two fivefold sets.
In the "Incremental One" (Ekottarika), it is established that stealing is completed when the six factors are present, thereby constituting the offense of theft.
As for the latter three or five phrases, the offense is established through the presence of the intent to steal;
therefore, they are not mentioned within the "Incremental Six."
From the section on "The Ground" (*bhūmi*) onwards,
the second part clarifies the methodological application of the perfection of stealing (*steya-pāramitā*).
First, twenty-six topical headings (*dvāra*) are listed.
These will be explained one by one later.
Within each chapter, there are seven phrases.
The first clarifies the location.
First, list the objects;
second, clarify the owner;
third, clarify the intent to steal.
Five, the fulfillment of the act of stealing;
six, the methods for stealing;
seven, the determination of the offense.
This first chapter contains these seven phrases;
the same applies to the subsequent chapters.
From "seeking by means of expedients more than five coins" onwards...
The third essential point concerns taking objects with intentionality;
it consists of thirty-six phrases,
which can be understood by examining the text.
The Vinaya text states:
"One who seeks by means of stratagems more than five coins.
This clarifies that it extends downward to include obtaining eleven coins.
If he obtains five coins, his original intention is fulfilled and he incurs a grave offense;
therefore, since six coins remain,
he then gives rise to the thought of taking these six coins.
Therefore, one further incurs a grave offense.
This constitutes the commission of two grave offenses.
If one obtains nine coins, one incurs one grave offense and one *sthūlātyaya* offense.
The first five constitute grave offenses;
because the latter four can suffice for others to complete an offense,
the latter four separately incur light offenses.
If one employs skillful means to seek five coins or more than five coins,
but does not obtain them, there is no offense;
however, the preparatory effort constitutes a heavy sthūlātyaya.
If one obtains four coins but does not fulfill the original intent of the mind,
one commits a heavy *sthūlātyaya* of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*).
If the four coins are obtained and come into the hand, one commits a heavy *sthūlātyaya* of the consummation (*niṣṭhā*).
If one obtains three *māṣaka* coins or less,
one commits a light *sthūlātyaya* of ultimate transgression.
The text states:
If one employs skillful means to seek less than five *kārsāpaṇas* but obtains more than five,
this constitutes a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*) from ten *kārsāpaṇas* downward;
in the former four cases, the original intent is fulfilled, resulting in a light offense.
The latter six cases constitute separate grave offenses (*sthūlātyaya*).
If one acquires six coins, this already exceeds five;
why wait for ten?
If one obtains six coins, this constitutes exceeding the limit of five;
yet, having obtained only two, there is only a light offense.
How is it known that a grave offense cannot be established?

Examining the text and verifying the principle, one may seek the fundamental essentials through one's own understanding: if the mind takes up [the object] and it is moved from its original location, it constitutes a light offense;
if the latter two types of intention arise and the object is taken up, they likewise constitute a light offense.
One cannot combine the preceding and succeeding [actions] to constitute a grave offense.
Why is this? Because the essential matters of the preceding and succeeding [moments] are distinct.
Therefore, they cannot be combined.
Even if one seeks to reduce [the value] by five *māṣakas* through expedient means and obtains five *māṣakas*,
this amounts to nine *māṣakas*.
If explained in detail, it is as above.
If one steals with a deliberate intent and the value is less than five coins,
once the object has entered one's hand, one commits the ultimate offense of *sthūlātyaya*.
If one does not commit the preparatory offense of *dukkaṭa* requiring threefold confession,
the text states:
"The recipient takes five coins."
If one takes another object from another location,
such that the recipient of the object incurs a grave offense while the instructor incurs a light offense; or...
The intent of the one who receives the instruction is to clearly understand the taking of this object; it is not that the gravity of the offense differs for the instructor.
Thus, the instructor incurs a light offense.
It is not because one incurs the offense of obtaining an object from the side of the object obtained;
rather, the offense is incurred at the point where the original intention was formed.
The phrase "different objects" clarifies that the objects are distinct.
"Being in different places" means that the persons are distinct.
The next two lines below refer to cases where neither party understands the other's language;
therefore, they mutually incur either light or heavy offenses. Question:
If one errs regarding stolen property, it may not constitute an offense;
yet, even if one errs regarding the precept against killing, one still commits an offense.
Why are these two cases not the same?
The answer is:
It may be that the stolen object has no owner;
furthermore, if one realizes it was taken by mistake, it can be returned to the rightful owner.
The precept against killing is not like that.
Since there is no one who lacks the knowledge of life yet considers another to be a human being,
how could there be any possibility of error?
Furthermore, regarding the cessation of life, one knows that there is no returning to life;
while error may indeed be possible in principle—
such as when intending to kill a person before, the arrow mistakenly strikes a person behind— it is not so here.
This may not constitute an offense;
therefore, it is not the same as theft. Question:
The owner of the property is one and the same.
Question: If one steals a large amount of money in a single instance, how many grave offenses are committed? Answer:
One commits one grave offense. Question: [What if...]
If that were so, then killing many people at once would also result in only a single offense. Answer:
It is not so; for theft, the primary harm is to the owner, and the owner is a single individual.
Killing is the taking of life;
since persons are each distinct,
how can they be one and the same?
The last eight lines consist of four preceding lines concerning offenses involving five *kārsāpaṇas* or more,
and four subsequent lines concerning offenses involving less than five *kārsāpaṇas*.
One who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged should be considered afflicted;
these four types of persons do not commit an offense because it is intended to clarify that such individuals, due to this severe illness, have no self-recollection whatsoever.
Because of this, that bhikṣu does not commit an offense.
If one takes five coins from an ownerless object while perceiving it as having an owner,
one commits the grave sthūlātyaya offense of preparatory action.
The offense is grave because it arises from the mind;
when one suspects that an object with an owner is actually ownerless,
both of these cases constitute the offense of taking five coins.
The preparatory offense (prayoga) is a light sthūlātyaya;
it is light because of the doubt in the mind.
If one obtains four *kārsāpaṇas* by means of theft from property that has an owner, [the full offense is incurred].
If one commits the act with the full amount of four coins, one incurs a grave *sthūlātyaya*;
if it is less than four coins, one incurs a light *sthūlātyaya*.
This applies even if one perceives what is ownerless as having an owner.
If one takes less than five *māṣaka* coins, one commits an offense of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of a heavy nature; the consummation (*niṣṭhā*) is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This applies whether there is doubt regarding the object having an owner or doubt regarding its being ownerless.
If these two items are taken when their value is less than five māsakas,
one commits the preparatory offense of *dukkaṭa*.
Although it is light, one must nevertheless perform three recitations of repentance before another person.
If one steals five *kārsāpaṇa* from a non-human being while perceiving it as a non-human being,
one commits a *sthūlātyaya* that is slightly lighter than the ultimate offense;
if one steals four *kārsāpaṇa* from a human being, [the same applies].
If it is indeed refuse material and one takes five *kārsāpaṇas* while perceiving them as belonging to a non-human being,
one commits a grave *duṣkṛta* offense of preliminary effort requiring threefold confession.
This also applies if there is doubt that they belong to a non-human being or doubt that they are ownerless property.
If one steals these two items and obtains five coins,
one commits the offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) through the preliminary effort, which is slightly lighter.
This applies if one perceives what is not a person as not being a person.
If one steals four *kārsāpaṇa* coins by means of deliberate intent,
one commits a grave *duṣkṛta* offense requiring a single confession.
If one acquires less than four *kārsāpaṇa* coins, it is likewise [a *duṣkṛta*].
Violating this constitutes a light offense of *dukkaṭa*, which is also expiated through a single confession.
If one takes an object belonging to no owner while perceiving it as not belonging to a human being, and the value is less than five *māṣaka* coins, [it is likewise a light offense].
If it is not a person, but rather an object of doubtful ownership,
these three cases all constitute the light preparatory offense of *duṣkṛta*.
If one steals an animal belonging to another and its value reaches five *māṣakas*, [it constitutes a full offense].
If one commits the offense to its full extent, it is a *duṣkṛta* requiring one confession;
taking less than five *māṣakas* is likewise one confession.
Although there is a different category of *duṣkṛta*, this is the most minor of offenses.
It is simply because there is no other basis for remorse.
It is exactly like a thief who, having stolen five coins, commits an offense requiring expulsion (*pārājika*);
even if the object belonged to a single owner worth hundreds of thousands, how could it not be grave? Furthermore, it is on account of such expulsion that [the offense] is considered weighty.
Furthermore, because there is no other method for purifying such offenses,

The fourth time, based on the initial denial of the previous two times,

The second explanation is that because noble persons possess two kinds of truthful speech,

What are these two kinds of truthful speech?
When the Sage’s body and mind realize the realm of phenomena, both mind and object are real;

Second, there is speech that describes objects according to the perceptions of the mind.
It is not necessarily as Maudgalyāyana predicted—that seven days would pass;

Ordinary persons lack the words of truth that constitute the first body of realized dharma.

Ordinary worldlings also possess a small degree of truthful speech regarding their own bodies and minds;

In these two types of false speech, they constitute lying provided that the object and the mind are both merely deceptive. This is because,
in these two cases of false speech,

It is difficult to verify whether [a matter] is true or false; therefore,

How can the objects and events experienced by a predecessor be verified?

One claims to have attained the state of an Arya;

Although the nature of an object—whether it is real or illusory—is difficult to discern, there may be cases where one need not rely on another's own words; rather, by drawing out the falsehood and directly verifying it, the truth can be known.
